summary: Updated the CDK example to v2 and distinguished supported developer services from retired CodeStar and OpsWorks and restricted Cloud9.

sources.title: AWS OpsWorks Stacks end of life

changes.find: Once you have the dependencies installed, you can execute this Python script, and it will create the S3 bucket in your AWS account based on the code defined in the `MyS3BucketStack` class.
changes.replace: This CDK v2 example synthesizes a template. It does not create resources until you bootstrap the target environment where required and run `cdk deploy`. Keep the default retention behavior for stored data.

```python
from aws_cdk import App, Stack
from aws_cdk import aws_s3 as s3
from constructs import Construct

class MyS3BucketStack(Stack):
    def __init__(self, scope: Construct, construct_id: str, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(scope, construct_id, **kwargs)
        s3.Bucket(self, "MyS3Bucket", versioned=True)

app = App()
MyS3BucketStack(app, "MyS3BucketStack")
app.synth()
```

changes.find: - Just the application code is the responsibility of the developer
changes.replace: - Customers remain responsible for application code, data, access policies, configuration, and keeping the chosen platform branch supported. Managed platform updates are configurable, not a blanket removal of patching responsibilities.

changes.find: - Servers / Instances must be provisioned and configured ahead of time with the CodeDeploy Agent
changes.replace: - EC2 and on-premises deployments need the CodeDeploy agent. CodeDeploy also supports Lambda and ECS deployments through their supported deployment configurations.

changes.find: - Private, Secured, Integrated with AWS
changes.replace: - Private, secured, and integrated with AWS. CodeCommit reopened to new customers on 25 November 2025; older closed-to-new-customer notices are no longer current.

## AWS CodeStar

Historical service: AWS CodeStar ended support in 2024. Use supported individual developer tools, such as CodePipeline, CodeBuild, and CodeDeploy. CodeStar's retirement does not mean CodeStar Connections/AWS CodeConnections or those separate services have retired.

changes.find: - AWS Cloud9 is a cloud IDE (Integrated Development Environment) for writing, running and debugging code
changes.replace: - AWS Cloud9 is a browser IDE for existing customers. It has been closed to new customers since 25 July 2024; new users should choose supported local development tools or AWS CloudShell for browser-based CLI tasks.

changes.find: - If an instance can’t be controlled with SSM, it’s probably an issue with the SSM agent!
changes.replace: - Check SSM Agent, IAM instance permissions, network access to the required endpoints, and the managed-node configuration when a system is not reachable.

## AWS OpsWorks

Historical service: The AWS OpsWorks services ended support in 2024. Do not choose OpsWorks for a new deployment. Evaluate AWS Systems Manager for supported configuration/patch automation and the software vendor's supported Chef or Puppet deployment options.

### OpsWorks Architecture

The original diagram below describes the retired service and is retained only to explain older material.

![Historical OpsWorks architecture](../images/OpsWorks_Architecture.png)

changes.find: - OpsWorks (hybrid): managed Chef and Puppet in AWS
changes.replace: - OpsWorks: retired managed Chef/Puppet and stack-management services, retained as historical context.

changes.find: - CodeStar: Unified view for allowing developers to do CICD and code
changes.replace: - CodeStar: retired; use supported individual CI/CD services.

changes.find: - Cloud9: Cloud IDE (Integrated Development Environment) with collab
changes.replace: - Cloud9: browser IDE for existing customers; closed to new customers.

summary: Corrected serverless definitions, EC2 scaling, Lambda runtime and container support, and pricing assumptions.

changes.find: - **Two launch modes**: **EC2** (self-managed instances) and **Fargate** (serverless).
changes.replace: - Core compute choices include customer-managed EC2 instances and Fargate. ECS also offers managed-instance and external-capacity options; distinguish orchestration from responsibility for the host.

changes.find: - Serverless was pioneered by AWS Lambda but now also includes anything that’s managed: “databases, messaging, storage, etc.”
changes.replace: - A managed service is not automatically serverless. For example, provisioned RDS instances still have capacity and instance choices; Lambda and Fargate remove host-server management for their supported workloads.

changes.find: | Scaling means intervention to add / remove servers | Scaling is automated!                     |
changes.replace: | EC2 Auto Scaling can add and remove instances automatically | Lambda scales supported invocations subject to concurrency and service quotas |

changes.find:
- Go
- .NET Core
changes.replace:
- Go through a supported OS-only/custom runtime (the old managed go1.x runtime is deprecated)
- Supported .NET runtimes

changes.find: - custom runtime (via container images) (community supported, example Rust)
changes.replace: - Other languages through a custom runtime that implements the Lambda Runtime API; supported container images are another packaging option.

changes.find: - It is usually **very cheap** to run AWS Lambda so it’s **very popular**
changes.replace: - These figures describe a conventional request/duration pricing example, not a quote for every configuration. Architecture, Region, usage tiers, provisioned concurrency, extra ephemeral storage, and newer execution options can change cost. Check current Lambda pricing and Free Tier account eligibility.

changes.find: - **Throttling**, **caching**, and **authorization** features built-in.
changes.replace: - Features depend on API type. For example, API Gateway's built-in API cache is a REST API feature; do not assume HTTP and WebSocket APIs provide the same features.

changes.find: - Language Support: many programming languages except (arbitrary) Docker
changes.replace: - Lambda supports runtime-compatible container images. It is not a service for arbitrary long-running containers; use ECS/Fargate for those workloads.

changes.find: - ECR: Private Docker Images Repository
changes.replace: - ECR: managed private and public container-image repositories.

summary: Removed stale edge counts and an unsupported speed percentage; corrected CloudFront OAC, replication, Route 53 aliases, and transfer acceleration.

changes.find: - example.com => AWS resource == Alias (ex: ELB, CloudFront, S3, RDS, etc…)
changes.replace: - example.com => supported AWS alias target, such as an ELB load balancer, CloudFront distribution, or S3 website endpoint. An RDS DB instance endpoint is not a general Route 53 alias target; use an appropriate CNAME on a non-apex name.

changes.find: - 216 Point of Presence globally (edge locations)
changes.replace: - Uses AWS's global edge network. The number of locations changes; check current AWS infrastructure information instead of memorizing an old count.

changes.find: - Enhanced security with CloudFront Origin Access Identity (OAI)
changes.replace: - Prefer CloudFront origin access control (OAC) for a supported private S3 origin. OAI is the older mechanism and has feature limitations.

changes.find:
| Files are cached for a TTL (Time to Live) (maybe a day)        | Files are updated in near real-time, Read only                                         |
| **Great for static content that must be available everywhere** | **Great for dynamic content that needs to be available at low-latency in few regions** |
changes.replace:
| Cached objects follow cache-control and TTL settings | Replication asynchronously copies eligible objects between versioned buckets |
| Useful for cached content delivery near viewers | Useful for compliance, data locality, and resilience; replicas are objects, not a dynamic application or a universally read-only database |

changes.find: - if we try to upload file to Australia S3 bucket it will take time using CloudFront we can rescue time.
changes.replace: - S3 Transfer Acceleration is a separate S3 transfer feature that uses edge locations; do not confuse it with a CloudFront distribution.

changes.find: - Leverage the AWS internal network to optimize the route to your application (60% improvement)
changes.replace: - Uses the AWS network to optimize paths to supported endpoints. Actual improvement depends on client location and network conditions; there is no guaranteed 60% speedup.

changes.find: - No additional charges or service agreements
changes.replace: - Wavelength usage is billed according to its supported services and pricing. Connectivity, carrier, and parent-Region requirements must be considered; it is not a blanket no-charge deployment.

summary: Clarified Cognito user pools versus identity pools, expanded workforce federation, and identified Simple AD's new-customer restriction.

changes.find: - Instead of creating IAM users, create users in Cognito
changes.replace: - User pools provide application sign-up, sign-in, and tokens. Identity pools exchange supported identities for temporary AWS credentials. Cognito serves application users; IAM Identity Center serves workforce access.

changes.find: - Cannot be joined with on-premise AD
changes.replace: - Does not provide an AD trust relationship to on-premises Microsoft AD. Simple AD is closed to new customers; evaluate AWS Managed Microsoft AD or AD Connector according to the requirement.

changes.find: - Built-in identity store in IAM Identity Center
changes.replace: - Built-in identity store, supported external identity providers, or supported Microsoft Active Directory integration.
